quiz.q: A company uses MuleSoft's Runtime Manager, API Manager and Exchange, but its Mule runtimes run on its own servers. Which deployment model is this?
quiz.explain: Hybrid = MuleSoft control plane + your own runtime plane. On-premises would mean the control plane is also your own.

quiz.q: A bank runs Mule runtimes in its own AWS account (Indian region) and manages them from MuleSoft's Runtime Manager. Which model is it?
options: CloudHub, because it runs on AWS
quiz.explain: The runtime is self-managed even though it's in the cloud, so it's hybrid. In CloudHub, MuleSoft itself has made the cloud Mule-ready and manages it.

quiz.q: Which components belong to the control plane?
quiz.explain: The control plane manages Mule apps: Runtime Manager, API Manager and Exchange (the Anypoint Management Center). The runtime plane is the Mule runtime, connectors and logs.

quiz.q: According to the instructor, why don't Indian banks use CloudHub?
options: There was no CloudHub region in India, and RBI rules require banking data to stay in India
quiz.explain: It's about data residency, not a cloud ban: without an in-country region, data and logs would be stored outside India.

quiz.q: An app is deployed on two workers behind a load balancer. What is the main reason for the second worker?
options: Each request is processed twice as fast
High availability — if one worker goes down, traffic goes to the other
quiz.explain: Processing speed doesn't improve; the main reason is high availability. The load balancer automatically sends all traffic to the healthy worker.

quiz.q: With round-robin load balancing and 2 workers, how are requests 1, 2, 3, 4 distributed?
options: All to worker 1 until it is full
To whichever worker has the least CPU
quiz.explain: Round robin distributes requests in turn, so with 1,000 requests a day each worker handles about 500.

quiz.q: Your CloudHub app goes through a Dedicated Load Balancer over HTTPS. Which listener port does it need?
Which statement about the Shared Load Balancer is correct?
options: It is premium and configured by your team
It is used by many companies in CloudHub and provided by default
Only your organisation's traffic goes through it
quiz.explain: The SLB is shared by many customers and provided by default. The DLB is the premium one dedicated to your organisation.

quiz.q: Each worker handles ~5,000 requests/day. A festive week brings 20,000/day. What does the class suggest?
options: Scale up to about 5 workers, then scale down afterwards
quiz.explain: Scale up (e.g. 5 workers = 25,000 capacity with headroom) in Runtime Manager, then scale back down to 2–3 after the festival.

quiz.q: What is auto-scaling in this lecture?
options: A free default that adds workers on every deployment
A premium feature that adds/removes workers based on traffic
Moving an app between regions automatically
quiz.explain: Auto-scaling needs extra licensing; without it you increase workers manually in Runtime Manager.

quiz.q: Who decides how many workers an application needs?
options: The developer, based on the number of flows
The architect, based on non-functional requirements and performance testing
quiz.explain: Architects use NFRs (traffic, policies) and performance testing; cost matters too since workers consume vCores.

quiz.q: What is special about Runtime Fabric (RTF)?
options: It runs only in MuleSoft's cloud
It runs in containers on your own servers, with MuleSoft applying patches and Mule updates automatically
It is always faster than CloudHub
quiz.explain: RTF runs on your infrastructure in containers, connected to MuleSoft's control plane; data and logs stay under your control. It isn't inherently faster.

cards.back: **CloudHub**, **on-premises**, **hybrid**, plus **Runtime Fabric**.
MuleSoft-managed cloud for running Mule apps: MuleSoft provides both the control plane and the runtime plane.
Own runtime **and** own control plane. Chosen by highly regulated industries; more secure, high cost and maintenance.
MuleSoft control plane + your own runtime (physical servers or your own cloud account).
Components that manage Mule apps: **Runtime Manager**, **API Manager**, **Exchange** (Anypoint Management Center).
Where the app executes: **Mule runtime**, connectors and components, logging.
The software that executes Mule applications — a Mule app runs on a server with the Mule runtime installed.

cards.front: How do you decide the deployment model?
cards.back: By who provides each plane: both MuleSoft → CloudHub; MuleSoft control + own runtime → hybrid; both own → on-premises.

cards.front: Why might a bank not use CloudHub?
cards.back: Data must stay in the country; with no CloudHub region there, data and logs would leave it. Such banks use hybrid or on-premises.
MuleSoft's Mule-ready infrastructure on top of cloud providers (AWS; the instructor also mentioned Azure).
A mini server in CloudHub where your Mule application runs. A trial account can use only **one** worker.
Geographic location of CloudHub infrastructure (e.g. US, Europe/London), chosen at deployment.
A facility housing servers. Some companies rent servers from data-centre businesses, like co-working office space.
Sits in front of multiple workers and decides which server receives each request.
Requests are distributed to servers in turn (most used method).
**High availability**: if one worker fails, the load balancer sends traffic to the others. Not faster requests.
Shared LB: many customers, provided by default. Dedicated LB: only your org, premium, configured by your team.
Adding/removing workers (in Runtime Manager in the cloud). On own servers it means buying and setting up hardware.
Premium feature that adds workers when traffic rises and removes them when it falls.
CPU/memory unit; MuleSoft charges by vCore, so more workers mean more cost.
The architect, using non-functional requirements and performance testing. Important apps get **at least two** workers.
Container-based runtime on your own servers; MuleSoft applies patches/updates automatically; connected to MuleSoft's control plane.
Technically MuleSoft's **Anypoint Platform Private Cloud Edition**. Many teams calling themselves on-prem are really hybrid.
